analyses.field: Detection of diffusion-generated portraits (reconstruction-error, noise-space, spectral, zero-shot, foundation-feature and aligned-pair methods; face-specific benchmarks; dataset-bias literature)
lessons: Data construction decides, not architecture. Since 2024 every leading method builds each fake as a reconstruction of a real image so the pair differs only in the generator trace: B-Free reports 96.3 balanced accuracy, 20.7 points above the next method (Guillaro et al., arXiv 2412.17671, Table 5); DDA reports 90.7 average over 11 benchmarks, 15.7 points above the next (Chen et al., arXiv 2505.14359). A 2026 study of 23 released detectors finds training-data alignment moves accuracy by 20 to 60 points inside one architecture family and the best detector reaches only 75.0% mean accuracy (Ren et al., arXiv 2602.07814, abstract).

Each fix exposes the next leftover cue: format and size (Grommelt et al., arXiv 2403.17608), then resampling direction (Rajan et al., arXiv 2410.11835, Fig. 2 and Table 5), then frequency content inside pixel-aligned pairs (DDA: a frequency detector flags 93% of visually identical reconstructions), then the generator's initial noise (Zhou et al., arXiv 2506.00874). No paper claims a bias-free detector; each shows one named cue is no longer used. Our claim should have the same form: a list of named cues, each with its control.

Reconstruction-error and inversion methods (DIRE arXiv 2303.09295; AEROBLADE arXiv 2401.17879, mean average precision 0.992; LatentTracer arXiv 2405.13360) test whether an image lies in the range of a generator. A one-photo reconstruction and a two-person morph from the same autoencoder both do, so this family cannot separate them and is useful to us only as a measure of generator trace.

A stochastic code obtained by inversion is not Gaussian noise; it keeps image structure, and mixing two such codes leaves a footprint of the mixing operation. Patch correlations 0.382 against 0.039 for noise and a quality dip in the middle of interpolation paths (Staniszewski et al., arXiv 2410.23530, Table 2 and Fig. 5); slerp is clean for model-generated images and leaves artefacts for natural ones (NoiseDiffusion, ICLR 2024, arXiv 2403.08840); a head silhouette is visible in the encoded code (Fast-DiM, arXiv 2310.09484). This explains why our probes read 'two codes were mixed' on diffusion renders and not a second person.

In a diffusion-autoencoder morph the contributors appear to sit mostly in the image-shaped stochastic code, not in the 512-number semantic code: with white noise in place of the encoded code, the share of morphs matching both contributors falls to 4.5 / 3.48 / 2.04% (Fast-DiM, arXiv 2310.09484, Table III). This is my reading of one table in an attack paper; it predicts that the readable signal is a double exposure of two head geometries, like a landmark blend.

The field is split, by task, on whether a one-photo reconstruction is real or fake. Generated-image detectors label it fake (DRCT, ICML 2024; Rajan et al.: 'can still be validly considered fake, at least for our task'; B-Free; DDA). Mandelli et al. (arXiv 2407.10736) make it a third class, 'laundered', separable from fully synthetic images at AUC 0.994 (Table I). Cannas et al. (arXiv 2412.03261, ICCV Workshops 2025) treat a neural-codec file of a real photo as real and count its flagging as a false alarm (up to 0.96 to 0.99 at 0.12 bits per pixel, Table 1). This supports our third category and reporting under both policies.

Separation inside one generator proves nothing about what is read: two image populations that share a decoder are separated at 0.994 by a patch CNN (Mandelli et al., Table I), and that detector's accuracy at a fixed threshold falls from 95.9 to 80.2% after a 0.5 times downscale (Table II). Our frozen-feature probe result on diffusion morphs (0.945 to 1.000, unreviewed) needs the same-person mix as its negative before it says anything about a second person.

A frozen foundation encoder is not a safety argument. Linear probes on new encoders lead in-the-wild sets (Chameleon 96.1 and 92.4 against 57.2 for the 2023 CLIP probe; Zhou et al., arXiv 2509.12995, Table 1), but the authors attribute the gain of the vision-language models to exposure to generated images in pretraining (Tables 4 and 5). There is no counterpart of that for morphs, and it matches our reviewed finding that a frozen-encoder release still follows storage history.

Cues tied to the 'real' class and cues tied to the 'fake' class need different remedies. Stay-Positive (Rajan and Lee, arXiv 2502.07778) removes real-side cues with a non-negative last layer (FLUX average precision 57.25 to 99.33, Table 1) and names fake-side cues such as upsampling as its open limitation. Our measured shortcut (softness and storage history raise the morph score) is on the fake side, so this remedy does not apply.

In morph detection the same families were tried without controls: generated-image detectors and frozen features reach near zero error within one source and 35.78 to 42.65% across sources, 56.55 to 60.50% after print and scan for the GAN-attribution features (Colbois and Marcel, IJCB 2024, arXiv 2410.16802, Tables 5 to 7), and that paper states the framing openly: 'treating MAD as a deepfake detection problem'. No morph paper pairs a morph with a one-photo reconstruction of the same generator.
shortcut_findings: File format: in GenImage the real images are JPEG (mostly quality 96) and the fakes PNG. A Midjourney-trained ResNet50 calls uncompressed FFHQ photos real in 80.45% of cases as PNG, 94.84% at JPEG 95 and 100.0% at JPEG 60 (Grommelt et al., arXiv 2403.17608, Table 2). Removal: train only on data with equal quality factor in both classes; accuracy on JPEG-95 inputs rises 53.91 to 67.17 (Table 3). AEROBLADE (arXiv 2401.17879, Sec. 9) reports the same storage bias in the public data of DIRE.

Image size: generators emit fixed sizes and real images vary. Removal by constrained subsets with overlapping sizes: cross-generator accuracy 71.68 to 82.74 (ResNet50) and 74.09 to 85.83 (Swin-T) with about a quarter of the training data (Grommelt et al.).

Resampling direction: fakes at 256 px against larger reals make a detector 'associate downsampling with real images and upsampling with fake images'; real accuracy 54.16 to 83.58 and fake accuracy 69.56 to 29.83 when everything is downsampled to 256 (Rajan et al., arXiv 2410.11835, Fig. 2 and Table 5). Removal: reconstruct each real image with the autoencoder at its own resolution, no resizing, and put each pair in one batch with identical augmentation.

A hidden codec: LSUN real images were WebP-compressed and stored as PNG, and detectors learned WebP as a sign of 'real' (Stay-Positive, arXiv 2502.07778). Removal: last-layer retraining with non-negative weights so real-side features cannot lower the score.

Semantic content: the same DALL·E 3 fakes get different scores depending on whether the real set is RAISE or COCO (B-Free, arXiv 2412.17671, Fig. 2). Removal: self-conditioned reconstruction plus local inpainting with the original background pasted back; ablation 61.9 (text-paired) to 80.7 (reconstruction) to 92.2-96.4 (with local edits) balanced accuracy, and calibration repaired (negative log-likelihood 1.91 to 0.10, Table 2). FakeInversion (CVPR 2024, arXiv 2406.08603) adds content-matched evaluation by reverse image search; Zheng et al. (NeurIPS 2024) shuffle patches.

Frequency content inside pixel-aligned pairs: a frequency detector flags 93% of visually identical autoencoder reconstructions, and masking a few high-frequency DCT coefficients removes the detection, because real images lost high frequencies to JPEG and the decoder restores them (DDA, arXiv 2505.14359, Fig. 5). Removal: give the reconstruction the JPEG history of its real image, plus pixel mixing, and test on a set built the same way (DDA-COCO).

Initial noise of the generator: for each of 1,000 prompts an initial noise exists that makes the output pass as real, often within about 10 optimisation steps (Zhou et al., arXiv 2506.00874). Removal: add such on-manifold examples to training; GenImage average 79.20 to 94.63 for CLIP with LoRA (Table 1).

Neural processing as a false-alarm source: one autoencoder pass makes detectors call real photos synthetic and drops camera-model identification from 96.15% to 39.08-56.67% (Mandelli et al., arXiv 2407.10736, Sec. V); neural compression does the same and retraining with 20% such images only lowers the false-alarm rate from 0.96 to 0.65 (Cannas et al., arXiv 2412.03261, Tables 1 and 4).

Pretraining exposure: new vision-language encoders match fakes to the words 'AI generated' (similarity 0.828 and 0.861) and reach only 27.4 and 44.4% real-image accuracy on private photos with newer generators (Zhou et al., arXiv 2509.12995, Tables 4 and 5). No removal offered.

The field shows its biases with transplant tests on whole sets; the closest thing to our ladder is one matched step (a real image against its own reconstruction). A ladder of several rungs per image is a finer instrument than the field has.

ideas.name: Common last hop: pass both classes through the unchanged autoencoder (audit protocol and training crossing)
ideas.source_technique: Laundering: one encoder-decoder pass overwrites the forensic history of a photo (Mandelli, Bestagini, Tubaro, arXiv 2407.10736; Cannas et al., JPEG AI, ICCV Workshops 2025, arXiv 2412.03261), and the same pass is what aligned-pair training uses to make the fake class (Rajan et al. arXiv 2410.11835; B-Free arXiv 2412.17671; DDA arXiv 2505.14359). Here it is turned round: the pass keeps the label and equalises the last processing step.
ideas.transfer: Let L be the pinned diffusion-autoencoder path run unchanged on one image, the operation that already makes rung R2 of the diffusion ladder. Audit use: apply L to both classes of a benchmark cell and to rungs R0, R1, R2w, R3, R4 of the landmark ladder, so every image is a 256 px lossless file from one decoder. A released detector whose separation collapses on the laundered cell was reading last-hop history; one that keeps it reads softness or geometry. Training use: cross the last-hop state (raw, laundered) with the label on the standard recipe; a laundered genuine photo goes to the single-subject class and is never called genuine or morph, a laundered two-person morph stays a morph. Under our constraints this is the one permitted operation that changes low-level statistics. Side instrument: render from the semantic code with fresh noise (no inversion needed); by Fast-DiM Table III this drops the contributors, so a detector that still separates a benchmark cell on such renders reads the cell's semantic composition, for example the smiling half. Published tables: the base recipe is unchanged; the MorDIFF cell may get worse because the decoder trace no longer helps, and is reported under both class policies.
ideas.why_shortcut_free: Cannot use file size, format, codec, chroma subsampling or resampling grid (equal after L by construction) and cannot use the generator fingerprint (both classes carry it). Ladder contrasts: L(R1) against L(R0) must not separate; R0 against L(R0) must not move the morph score after training; L(R4) against L(R3) must keep the signal. It does not remove softness; that still needs warped halves and the existing softened examples.
ideas.used_in_morph_detection_already: None found. Search 'morphing attack detection laundering OR regeneration OR purification autoencoder diffusion pass through generator bona fide reconstructed' returned only MAD-DDPM, MorDIFF and demorphing papers. Closest: one sentence in Zhang, Ramachandra, Raja, Busch (CVPR Workshops 2024, arXiv 2501.09817) on adding reconstructed bona fide images to GAN-morph sets (genuine side only, method not described, no test), and our own planned audit with GAN-reconstructed genuine photos (AG2).
ideas.first_test: About 2 A100 hours (about 22 hours on the shared DGX, so Athena or a cut to 20 hosts). Launder 100 hosts of the landmark ladder, OpenCV engine, rungs R0, R1, R2w, R3, R4 (500 images). Host-disjoint logistic probes on DINOv3 and CLIP features: (a) L(R1) against L(R0) beside R1 against R0; (b) L(R4) against L(R3) beside R4 against R3, each as excess over the Laplacian-variance floor; (c) flag rates of the SelfMAD and MADation releases on L(R0). Pass: (a) at or below 0.65 and (b) keeps at least 80% of its raw excess. Kill: (a) stays at or above 0.90 (the pass does not equalise storage history), or (b) falls below 0.60 (the pass erases the morph evidence itself).
ideas.risk: The autoencoder is trained on FFHQ at 256 px, so passport-style photos are partly out of domain and its aligner re-crops. The pass may soften sharp and soft inputs differently and create a new history cue (test (a) catches this). Softness survives the pass. Inversion costs about 13 s per image on an A100. The MorDIFF-cell number may fall. The much cheaper Stable Diffusion autoencoder is not on the approved list and would need the author's yes.

ideas.name: One network with three outputs; the morph score is the contrast against both non-morph classes
ideas.source_technique: Three-class treatment of processed images in generated-image forensics: pristine, laundered, fully synthetic (Mandelli et al., arXiv 2407.10736, Table I: 0.994 between the two generator classes); the call to separate harmless from harmful neural processing (Cannas et al., arXiv 2412.03261); the effect of training construction on calibration (B-Free, arXiv 2412.17671, Table 2: negative log-likelihood 1.91 to 0.10); paired batches (Rajan et al., arXiv 2410.11835).
ideas.transfer: One network, one softmax over the three categories of the class proposal: G genuine capture (R0, R1), S single-subject manipulation (R2, R2w, R3m, R3; generator rungs x1, x2; laundered genuine images), M two-person morph (R4, x3). The reported score is one number from one forward pass, s = log P(M) - log(P(G)+P(S)); no second stage, no gate. Train with whole within-host tuples in one batch and identical crops. A binary head must give a camera photo and a same-person morph the same output although they differ by the largest signal in the data (the pipeline step, read at 0.91 to 0.98 in the paired-difference experiment, PD1). A three-way head may represent that signal and route it to S, so a morph is flagged only when it beats both non-morph explanations. The single-subject table of the paper comes out of the same network as P(S). Published tables: only the head changes, so the benchmark score stays comparable.
ideas.why_shortcut_free: Storage history, warp, softness, pipeline and generator trace all have a class to go to that is not 'morph'. Ladder contrasts: s must not move from R0 to R1 or from R0 to R2w (limit 0.3 standard deviations, as for the alpha-field probe), and s must separate R4 from R3 and x3 from x2.
ideas.used_in_morph_detection_already: None found. Search 'face morphing attack detection three-class OR multi-class bona fide manipulated morph retouching single-subject manipulation separate class' returned only multi-class attribution of the morphing tool and a differential system that classifies the verification attempt (bona fide, criminal, accomplice). Our class-definition check found nobody who scores single-subject images with a label.
ideas.first_test: CPU, a few hours, cached features only: landmark ladder (536 hosts) and the diffusion-autoencoder blocks of the paired-difference experiment (PD1); five host-disjoint folds; multinomial three-way head against a binary logistic head with identical data and regularisation grid. Report AUC for R4 against R3 and x3 against x2 from s, the shift of s from R0 to R1 and to R2w, and EER of R4 against R0. Kill: no gain of at least 0.03 AUC on R4-against-R3 (or x3-against-x2) AND no halving of the R0-to-R1 or R0-to-R2w shift relative to the binary head; or genuine-against-morph EER on the landmark cells worse by more than 1 point.
ideas.risk: A linear head on frozen features may show no difference while a LoRA fine-tune would, so the cheap test can be underpowered. The S class is a mixed bag (warp, same-person mix, reconstruction). Soft two-person morphs may be drawn toward S and raise the miss rate. Single-subject images from tools we cannot run may land in M.

ideas.name: Code-factorial rungs and footprint-matched, step-crossed pairs for diffusion-autoencoder morphs
ideas.source_technique: Structure of inverted noise and artefacts of interpolating it (Staniszewski, Kuciński, Deja, arXiv 2410.23530; NoiseDiffusion, ICLR 2024, arXiv 2403.08840); the two codes of the diffusion autoencoder (Preechakul et al., arXiv 2111.15640); what each code carries in a morph (Fast-DiM, arXiv 2310.09484, Table III; DiM, arXiv 2301.04218); detectors leaning on the generator's noise state (Zhou et al., arXiv 2506.00874).
ideas.transfer: New rungs made with the pinned generator and the existing interp() on other argument pairs: for host A, second photo A' and other person B, cross the semantic code from (A, A') or (A, B) with the stochastic code from (A, A') or (A, B). Two corners exist already (same-person mix, two-person morph); the two new corners carry the second person in one code only. Two swap rungs use no interpolation at all: semantic code of A with the stochastic code of A', and with that of B. All new rungs are diagnostics and enter no error rate. They decide which code carries the 'second identity' projection (0.793 on one fold in PD1); the field predicts the stochastic code, which would make the signal a double exposure of two head geometries, trainable as one concept with landmark blends. Training rule for the diffusion family: the negative of every two-person morph is a same-person mix with the same interpolation and step count, never a reconstruction alone, and decoding steps (20 and 100) are crossed with the label so sharpness carries no label information. Published tables: only the diffusion training data change; the MorDIFF cell is then scored by mixing evidence, not by the decoder trace.
ideas.why_shortcut_free: Cannot use the mixing footprint (present in positive and negative), the generator trace (both rendered) or sharpness (step-crossed; Laplacian floor subtracted). Ladder contrasts: two-person morph against same-person mix at equal steps (x3 against x2); reconstruction against camera photo (x1 against x0) must not separate.
ideas.used_in_morph_detection_already: None found for the rungs or the rule. Searches 'morphing attack detection DDIM inversion OR inverted noise OR stochastic code OR latent inversion' and 'morphing attack detection StyleGAN style mixing OR noise inputs OR stochastic control latent morph versus single latent reconstruction' returned only generator papers (DCMorph, arXiv 2604.21627; DiM and Fast-DiM vary which code is interpolated to make stronger morphs) and differential demorphing (SFDemorpher, arXiv 2603.28322).
ideas.first_test: Minutes of GPU, no new inversion: the full run of the identical-and-mirrored-inputs check (AD1b) encodes the stochastic codes of A, A' and B for 16 persons. Render the four corners and two swaps at 20 steps (96 images); score with the heads of the paired-difference experiment (PD1) and its two-person-against-same-person projection; paired sign test per factor. Pass: one factor moves the projection in the expected direction in at least 13 of 16 persons (one-sided binomial p = 0.011). Kill: neither factor reaches 12 of 16 (p = 0.038); and on the larger Athena set (DG1, 536 hosts) two-person against same-person mix at equal steps stays below 0.65 after the Laplacian floor is subtracted. Then diffusion cells are reported as 'mixing is detected, a second person is not' for every detector including ours.
ideas.risk: n = 16 is small. FRLL same-person pairs differ in expression; FRGC and colorFERET second photos are the cleaner source. With a second person in one code only, the image may not match both contributors in face recognition, so no off-diagonal rung may be called a morph without that check. Whether calling the unchanged generator with new argument pairs counts as 'run unchanged' needs the author's yes.

ideas.name: Alignment by selection, with a frequency-only certificate and paired batches (upgrade of the SMDD rebuild)
ideas.source_technique: Constrained subsets with overlapping nuisance values (Grommelt et al., 'Fake or JPEG?', arXiv 2403.17608: cross-generator accuracy up 11 points with a quarter of the data); the finding that pixel-aligned pairs are still separable by frequency content, with a test set built to check it (DDA, arXiv 2505.14359); paired batches with identical augmentation (Rajan et al., arXiv 2410.11835).
ideas.transfer: The field equalises cues by processing images; we may not write new blur, resize or JPEG code, so we equalise by choosing and weighting images that exist. Measure a cue vector per image (file size, Laplacian variance with three kernel sizes, eight radial spectrum bands, border fraction, chroma subsampling, history flag, expression label). Fit a cue-only classifier of the label on the training pool, then weight samples by clipped inverse propensity or match them coarsely until the weighted cue-only AUC is at most 0.55. Train the standard recipe with whole within-host tuples per batch and identical crops. Print the certificate in the paper: cue-only AUC on the weighted training pool and on every evaluation cell, and the DDA check, a radial-spectrum-only probe inside matched pairs (R4 against R3, x3 against x2). This improves item 1 of the round-2 chain and the round-1 reweighting idea; it is not a new architecture. Published tables: less effective data; the field's precedent is that matched subsets generalise better, and the cost on FRLL cells is reported.
ideas.why_shortcut_free: The named cues (file attributes, softness, spectrum, border, expression, history) are at chance in the training pool by measurement, not by assumption. Ladder contrast: R0 against R1 at the fixed threshold; frequency-only probe at chance inside R4-against-R3 pairs.
ideas.used_in_morph_detection_already: None found as a measured property of a training set. Equal processing of both classes exists as evaluation practice (Zhang et al., CVPR Workshops 2024, arXiv 2501.09817: both classes printed, scanned and compressed to at most 15 KB). A 2026 search for morph detection with dataset bias or shortcuts returned only fairness and continual-learning papers.
ideas.first_test: CPU, hours: cue vectors from the existing cue checks; fit the cue-only model on the SMDD rebuild arms and the ladders; then a weighted against an unweighted logistic head on cached CLIP features. Kill: the cue-only AUC cannot be brought to 0.60 or below while keeping an effective sample size of at least 30% (the classes do not overlap in cue space, so only generated controls can work), or the weighted head does not at least halve the R0-to-R1 flag-rate change at the fixed threshold.
ideas.risk: Only named cues are balanced; an unlisted cue stays. Softness is tied to blending physically (0.52 times Laplacian variance), so overlap in sharpness needs the existing soft genuine images and warped halves in the pool. Weights can explode and the effective data shrink.

does_not_transfer: Reconstruction error and inversion as the detector (DIRE, AEROBLADE, LaRE2, FIRE, DNF): they ask whether the generator can reproduce the image, which is true for a one-photo reconstruction and for a morph; they need the attacker's generator at test time; in morph detection the sign of the error already differs between models (Colbois and Marcel, arXiv 2410.16802). Useful only as a covariate that measures generator trace.

Labelling every reconstruction as fake (DRCT, Rajan et al., B-Free, DDA): their task is the decoder trace, ours is the second person. Adopting the label would call a single-subject image a morph, which our rules count as an error.

Stay-Positive, the non-negative last layer (arXiv 2502.07778): it removes cues tied to the real class. Our measured shortcut is on the other side (softness and storage history raise the morph score), and the paper names exactly this as its open limitation.

Blur, JPEG and resize augmentation and DDA's JPEG alignment: not allowed under our constraints, and Grommelt et al. (arXiv 2403.17608) find random JPEG augmentation does not remove the format bias anyway.

Patch shuffling and patch voting against semantic bias (Zheng et al., NeurIPS 2024; Mandelli's 96 px patches): they push the detector toward local texture, which is where softness and storage history live; a second person is a property of the whole face.
Native-resolution multi-crop testing with averaged logits (B-Free, SPAI): averaging crops is score fusion, and a crop does not contain the face.

Training-free statistics (ZED, RIGID, score-curvature methods): they measure distance from camera-image statistics; a history-matched genuine photo is also off those statistics, and a morph of two camera photos need not be.

Foundation-model linear probes as a safety argument: the field's own explanation for their success is exposure to generated images in pretraining (arXiv 2509.12995), which has no counterpart for morphs; our record already shows a frozen encoder follows storage history.

On-manifold adversarial training as published (arXiv 2506.00874): it needs a nuisance latent that carries no label. In the diffusion autoencoder the stochastic code carries the contributors (Fast-DiM Table III), and StyleGAN3 has no noise inputs. Only the measurement transfers (a flip rate under nuisance-only variants on disk), not the training.
Scale (thousands of generators, Community Forensics) and provenance or watermarking (SynthID-Image): three days and few morphing tools; and the attacker makes the image.

analyses.field: Face anti-spoofing (presentation attack detection: print, replay and mask attacks in single images), including NIST's operational evaluation and the ISO/IEC 30107-3 error-rate view
lessons: Treat the classes asymmetrically: make only the bona fide class domain-independent and leave attacks spread out. SSDG reports leave-one-out HTER 7.38% against 11.19% without its bona-fide-only adversarial term (Jia et al., CVPR 2020, Table 1, arXiv 2004.14043); IADG whitens bona fide features more strongly than attack features (Zhou et al., CVPR 2023, arXiv 2304.05640); PatchNet uses margin 0.4 for bona fide and 0.1 for attack classes (Wang et al., CVPR 2022, arXiv 2203.14325).

Align the decision, not the features, and align the offset too. SA-FAS keeps domains as separate clusters and forces one bona-fide-to-attack direction (Sun et al., CVPR 2023, arXiv 2303.13662); GD-FAS shows that aligned weights still leave the bias, hence the threshold, misaligned, with calibration error 3.39 against 18.12 for SA-FAS on the first split (Jung et al., ICCV 2025, Table 2, arXiv 2507.04006). This is the field's name for our fixed-threshold failure.

Domain shift lives largely in per-image feature statistics (channel mean and spread, called style). The field shuffles them (SSAN, Wang et al., CVPR 2022, arXiv 2203.05340), whitens them per instance (IADG), or projects a test image's statistics onto learned bases with no model update (Zhou et al., CVPR 2024, arXiv 2403.19334).

The benchmark gain since 2023 comes from the CLIP image encoder, and a frozen encoder is not enough. FLIP's ablation: average HTER 25.86% from scratch, 6.00% from ImageNet weights, 3.48% from CLIP weights (Srivatsan et al., ICCV 2023, Table 5, arXiv 2309.16649); FoundPAD: frozen encoder with linear head 31.89% against 16.81% with low-rank adaptation (Ozgur et al., WACV Workshops 2025, Table 5, arXiv 2501.02892). MADation is the same recipe.

The face is incidental to these detectors. A detector trained only on print and replay recordings of 78 vegetables reaches 14.15% HTER and 92.70% AUC on average over four face benchmarks, better than training on synthetic faces at 27.56% and 81.02% (Ozgur, Boutros, Damer, ACM MM Workshops 2026, Table 2, arXiv 2608.21455). It is the anti-spoofing counterpart of our paired-differences result that a head trained on one-person mixes detects two-person morphs equally well.

Operational evaluation fixes the threshold in advance and reports per attack type and per sub-population. NIST tested 82 algorithms on about 20,000 attacks and 21,218 sequestered bona fide stills with two fixed points, APCER at BPCER 0.01 and BPCER at APCER 0.01, and read bona fide error per demographic group at one threshold fixed on a reference group (Ngan, Grother, Hom, NIST IR 8491, 2023, doi 10.6028/NIST.IR.8491).

Matched cue-removal controls belong in the evaluation. NIST scored print and replay attacks with and without the visible frame and hands (1,417 stills each): best APCER at BPCER 0.01 goes from 0.0 to 0.005 in the impersonation task and from 0.009 to 0.06 in the evasion task, and errors rise for all algorithms (NIST IR 8491, Tables 1, 2 and 5). This is our ladder in another field.

Every identity must appear under every class, or the model learns identity and background. UniAttackData was built on this rule after merged sets failed it; its leave-one-attack-type-out protocol stays hard at 22.42 ± 10.57% ACER (Fang et al., IJCAI 2024, Table 3, arXiv 2401.17699). SMDD breaks this rule by design.

One-sided supervision generalises better to unseen attacks: regress a cue map to zero on bona fide images only and give attacks no map target. On the unseen-attack-type protocol of SiW this gives 1.19% ACER against 7.66 to 12.10% for three earlier methods, and an all-one target for attacks was worse (Feng et al., arXiv 2005.03922, Table 1).

Academic reporting hides threshold drift, and morph detection already has one industrial measurement of it. SA-FAS shows 5.95% HTER at the best epoch against 14.36% as the mean of the last ten epochs (Tables 1 and 2), and HTER is often taken at the test set's own EER threshold (stated in arXiv 2608.21455). Marriott's NIST IFPC 2025 slides show a morph detector's false alarms at a fixed threshold rising under compression, and that a file-size-dependent threshold 'does not help much' (https://pages.nist.gov/ifpc/2025/presentations/30.pdf); our audit claim must be worded with that in view.
shortcut_findings: Face-free training works: trained on vegetables only, the standard CLIP-with-LoRA detector reaches 92.70% mean AUC on four face benchmarks, so the detectors read the recapture process and not faces; an ImageNet backbone on the same data gets 36.97% HTER, so the pretraining carries the result (Ozgur, Boutros, Damer, arXiv 2608.21455, Table 2). Remedy proposed there: use such data as a reference and as extra training data (multi-source AUC 92.11 to 96.96%, Table 4).

Resolution, blur and camera are named as the easy cues but were not measured: SA-FAS says a plain classifier may exploit 'the easiest difference (image resolution, blurriness, camera setting)' (arXiv 2303.13662, Sec. 3); FLIP's error analysis attributes real faces called attacks to low resolution and pixelisation (arXiv 2309.16649, Figures 4 and 6). Remedies: aligned decision direction (SA-FAS), aligned offset (GD-FAS, arXiv 2507.04006), feature-statistic shuffling or whitening (SSAN, IADG), and cross-face-resolution and cross-device protocols (GRAD-GPAD, arXiv 1904.06213).

Context is a measured cue: NIST's zoomed print and replay attacks raise errors for all 82 algorithms (NIST IR 8491); results are 'consistently better when the background is present' (Neto, Sequeira, Cardoso, WACV Workshops 2022, arXiv 2111.11127); PatchNet's score maps deviate at background and boundary regions (arXiv 2203.14325). Remedies: patches from the raw capture without resize, per-patch labels on patches shuffled between subjects (Kantarci et al., arXiv 2109.03484), and the paired with-and-without-context test.

Identity: merged data sets where no identity appears under all classes teach 'face ID, domain-specific information, and background' (Fang et al., arXiv 2401.17699). Remedies: identity-consistent data sets (UniAttackData and its extension, arXiv 2505.13327), liveness and identity features made orthogonal (Yang et al., arXiv 2407.08243), patch swapping between subjects (Fang et al., Pattern Recognition 2024, arXiv 2209.09035; the identity attribution there is argued, not tested).

Intra-data-set results do not survive pooling: with ten data sets relabelled by attack instrument, device, lighting and face resolution, no method generalised across instruments (ACER above 22% in all cross-data-set cases) and a quality-based detector had 17.03% HTER against 6.33% for a colour-texture one on the pooled test (Costa-Pazo et al., arXiv 1904.06213). Remedy: protocols that change one factor at a time, threshold fixed on a development set.

Frequency shortcuts: generalisation failure framed as reliance on easy frequency bands, countered by masking those bands in training (Cao and Ma, WACV 2025, abstract level, https://mlanthology.org/wacv/2025/cao2025wacv-generalized). The vegetable study adds that the attack-minus-bona-fide spectrum changes sign between data sets, so no single spectral cue explains transfer.

Interventional audit outside faces: in voice anti-spoofing, applying MP3 coding, noise or silence blanking to one class moves EER from near 0% when the association matches between training and test to above 50% when it is inverted (Sahidullah et al., arXiv 2601.17782). Recommendation there: report how scores depend on such factors, not error rates alone.

Class-specific resampling is still used to win challenges: the second-placed entry of the 2024 unified attack challenge down-sampled live faces in one protocol and attack faces in the other (Yuan et al., CVPR Workshops 2024, arXiv 2404.06211). This is how a resolution shortcut is planted; the field has not flagged it.

Reporting remedies: mean and spread over the last epochs because best-snapshot numbers are optimistic (SA-FAS: 5.95 against 14.36% HTER); calibration error per domain because a good ranking hides a moved threshold (GD-FAS); fixed-point error rates on a large separate bona fide set and bona fide error per group at one threshold (NIST IR 8491).

ideas.name: History as style: remove per-image token statistics before the head
ideas.source_technique: Style-based domain generalisation in anti-spoofing: style is the channel-wise mean and spread of a feature map. SSAN separates and shuffles it (Wang et al., CVPR 2022, arXiv 2203.05340); IADG whitens the style-sensitive part per instance (Zhou et al., CVPR 2023, arXiv 2304.05640); test-time style projection replaces a test image's statistics by a mix of learned bases with no model update (Zhou et al., CVPR 2024, arXiv 2403.19334); CFPL builds style from per-layer mean and spread (Liu et al., CVPR 2024, arXiv 2403.14333).
ideas.transfer: Our measured shortcuts are mostly spatially uniform operations: shrink-and-enlarge history, storage size, global softness. A uniform operation moves all patch tokens of an image alike, which is a change of the image's own token mean and spread. Blending two persons is not uniform: detail is lost where the faces disagree and kept where they agree. So standardise each token channel over the face-hull patches of the same image, score patches, and pool the upper tail (mean of the top tenth), because the plain mean is zero by construction. Variant a projects the statistics onto bases learned from unprocessed camera photos instead of removing them. Variant b swaps statistics between images of the same class during training, which multiplies history diversity with no image operation. In the CLIP-with-LoRA recipe this is one normalisation step in front of a patch-token head; one network, one image, no gate.
ideas.why_shortcut_free: Cannot use storage history or global softness to the extent they are uniform: the R0 (camera photo) against R1 (same photo with shrink-and-enlarge history) contrast on FRLL and on softened copies of ladder hosts must fall to chance and the genuine score shift must stay within 0.3 standard deviations. Whole-photo capture sharpness is removed with it. It does not remove border (blank it), expression, backdrop, warp (R0 against R2w is read as before, warp-only images stay as negatives) or generator fingerprints; for GAN and diffusion morphs it only protects against history.
ideas.used_in_morph_detection_already: None found. Search: "morphing attack detection instance normalization OR style OR AdaIN OR feature statistics domain shift" returned only image-level style transfer with discriminators (Kashiani et al., IJCB 2023, arXiv 2308.10392) and print-scan texture synthesis. Also searched "morphing attack detection domain generalization single-side OR adversarial OR meta-learning OR style".
ideas.first_test: One day, CPU, cached DINOv3 ViT-L/16 patch tokens at 512. Step A (one hour): for the 204 FRLL photos and their history-matched frames, and the softened copies of 200 ladder hosts, compute the patch-wise token difference and the share removed by a per-image channel-wise shift and rescale. Step B (half a day): refit the patch heads of the alpha-field probe (AF0) on per-image standardised tokens with top-tenth pooling and compare with the raw-token fit. PASS: native-to-history genuine shift at most 0.3 standard deviations and at most half the raw value, at most 10% of history-matched photos flagged at the 5% threshold, warp-only against two-person morph (OpenCV-style engine) at least 0.97 AUC (raw first pass 0.9948). KILL: less than half of the history shift is removed in step A on both pools, or the shift is not halved in step B, or warp-only against two-person morph falls below 0.90.
ideas.risk: Blur changes textured patches more than flat ones, so part of the history shift is content-dependent and survives. Dividing by the spread can amplify noise in flat images. The softness that made landmark morphs easy is thrown away on purpose, so native error on published landmark cells can rise. ViT tokens mix information across patches.

ideas.name: One-threshold training: align the genuine side only, and align the offset
ideas.source_technique: Single-side domain generalisation, where only bona fide features pass the domain adversary (Jia et al., CVPR 2020, arXiv 2004.14043); aligned decision direction with kept domains (SA-FAS, Sun et al., CVPR 2023, arXiv 2303.13662); bias and threshold alignment with group-wise loss scaling and calibration error per domain (GD-FAS, Jung et al., ICCV 2025, arXiv 2507.04006); asymmetric margins (PatchNet, arXiv 2203.14325); bona fide error per group at one threshold (NIST IR 8491).
ideas.transfer: The failure we measured in released detectors is a moved genuine score at a fixed threshold, which this field calls bias misalignment across environments. A within-host paired fit aligns the direction but not the absolute genuine level across pools and histories. Environments here are genuine constructions (native photo, shrink-and-enlarge history, softened copy, warp-only) per photo pool. Three terms act on genuine images only: equal logits for all genuine versions of one host; equal mean and upper tail of genuine logits across environments; a tight margin for genuine and a loose one for morphs. Morphs get no alignment, only a margin above the genuine versions of their own host, because aligning morphs across engines pushes the network to what all engines share, which is softness. Read-out: BPCER per environment at one threshold fixed on native development photos, the spread between best and worst environment, and calibration error per environment. It is an upgrade of group-robust and invariant-risk ideas already on our table, with three changes from this field: genuine side only, the offset as an explicit target, calibration per environment.
ideas.why_shortcut_free: Cannot use any cue that changes between genuine versions of one photo: storage history and softness (R0 against R1 and softened copies) and warp (R0 against R2w); the test is the worst-environment BPCER at the fixed threshold. Unseen histories are read on a left-out construction. Expression, capture detail and backdrop are not touched by the loss and are equalised only by training on complete ladders where every host appears in every class; generator fingerprints are not addressed.
ideas.used_in_morph_detection_already: Partly: symmetric adversarial consistency between a training image and its augmented view exists (Kashiani et al., IJCB 2023, arXiv 2308.10392, with discriminators and logit and embedding consistency). Nothing genuine-side-only and nothing on offset or threshold alignment was found. Searches: "morphing attack detection adversarial domain gradient reversal OR domain discriminator OR domain-invariant single image morph"; "invariant risk minimization OR group DRO OR worst-group morphing attack detection" (no morph result). Our own record holds a failed small trial of a consistency loss and group weighting with 16 to 90 pairs.
ideas.first_test: One day, CPU, cached pooled CLIP ViT-L/14 and DINOv3 features; ladder hosts for training (camera photos, warp-only images, two-person morphs, softened copies of 200 hosts), folds by person, FRLL pool held out. Four heads on identical images: plain; plain plus softened genuine copies as negatives; plus the per-host orbit term; plus the offset term. Threshold at 5% of native training-pool photos; read BPCER on FRLL native photos, FRLL history-matched frames per family, held-out softened copies and warp-only images, and MACER on FRLL two-person morphs. PASS: worst-environment BPCER at most 10% and at most half that of the data-only head, with warp-only against two-person AUC lower by no more than 0.01. KILL: the loss heads do not bring the worst-environment BPCER below three quarters of the data-only head; then only the data arm is kept.
ideas.risk: On frozen pooled features the linear version equals the already proposed projection in soft form, so the first test may only confirm what is known; the real test is inside the LoRA fit. Alignment holds only for histories seen in training. Pairs exist only for our own ladder. An earlier small consistency trial failed.

ideas.name: Name the nuisance: a classifier over ladder rungs with two-person morph as one class
ideas.source_technique: Fine-grained class recognition in anti-spoofing: PatchNet replaces live against attack by one class per capture device and material, several of them bona fide, with asymmetric margins, and reports 1.88% against 6.25% ACER for the binary network on OULU-NPU protocol 1, two changes tested together (Wang et al., CVPR 2022, arXiv 2203.14325). Supported by the separability argument of SA-FAS (arXiv 2303.13662) and fine-grained class text in the CLIP line (TF-FAS, ECCV 2024).
ideas.transfer: One network with one softmax over construction classes: camera photo; stored-small or softened photo; warp-only image; mirror self-blend; same-person morph; two-person morph; for generator families also one-photo reconstruction, same-person latent mix and two-person latent morph. The reported attack score is the log-odds of the two-person classes against all others. The mass on single-subject classes is a second output reported separately, which is the three-way class proposal that awaits the author. Margins are tight for genuine classes and loose for manipulation classes. A binary head has only one place to put softness evidence, the morph side. With named classes softness is explained by the stored-small class, warp by the warp-only class and blending by the self-blend and same-person classes, and the two-person class must beat each. Every decision carries an audit trail of which class competed. In the CLIP recipe the class prototypes can be free weights or sentences that describe the construction.
ideas.why_shortcut_free: Cannot use softness alone (R1 has its own class), warp alone (R2w), blending alone (R3m and R3) or a generator fingerprint alone (one-photo reconstruction). The defining contrasts are same-person morph against two-person morph (R3 against R4) and same-person latent mix against two-person latent morph. Because every ladder host appears in every class, expression, capture detail, backdrop and photo pool are equal across classes by construction; a border must still be blanked in all classes.
ideas.used_in_morph_detection_already: Only on the attack side: a multi-class head that names the morphing algorithm (Zhang, Jia, Lyu, Li, Fusion-based Few-Shot Morphing Attack Detection and Fingerprinting, arXiv 2210.15510). No work with several genuine classes or a single-subject class was found. Search: "morphing attack attribution OR multi-class OR fine-grained classification morph type classification morphing tool fingerprint".
ideas.first_test: One day, CPU, cached features of the landmark ladder (8,294 images, two engines, two pools) plus softened copies of 200 hosts and the FRLL history-matched frames. Multinomial logistic head on six classes, folds by person in the FRGC and colorFERET pool, also leave-one-engine-out; FRLL never trained on. Baseline on identical images: binary head, two-person morph against everything else. Read same-person against two-person AUC with the attack log-odds, native-to-history shift and flag rate at the 5% threshold on FRLL, warp-only against two-person, and the confusion matrix. PASS: same-person against two-person at least 0.90 on both engines (the alpha-field probe head, which never saw a same-person morph, has 0.853 and 0.830) and at most 10% of history-matched photos flagged. KILL: the attack log-odds are within 0.01 AUC of the binary head and within a tenth of its history shift, or same-person against two-person stays below 0.85.
ideas.risk: A same-person morph and a two-person morph differ in degree, not in kind, so look-alike pairs will be confused and the class border follows our data's mix of sessions. On GAN ladders the same-person against two-person contrast is weak so far (0.65). More classes need more data per class. The class list is a ruling the author has not made yet.

ideas.name: One-sided zero map: genuine constructions regress to zero, morphs get no template
ideas.source_technique: One-sided cue-map learning in anti-spoofing: regress the map to all-zero on live images only, give attacks no map target, add a ranking loss between classes, score by map magnitude (Feng et al., Learning Generalized Spoof Cues, arXiv 2005.03922; 1.19% against 7.66 to 12.10% ACER on unseen attack types, Table 1; an all-one target for attacks was worse). Live-only variant with latent attack features: OC-SCMNet (Huang et al., CVPR 2024).
ideas.transfer: This is a repair of the blend-evidence map, not a new headline. The alpha-field probe fits a measured per-patch target, and review found that a global flag times an anatomy template also fits it; its first pass shifts warp-only images by 0.73 standard deviations on FaceMorpher. In the one-sided form there is no positive template. The only per-patch target is zero, placed on every genuine construction: photos, warp-only images of both engines, softened copies. The probe already has warp-only images of its own engine as zero targets, so the new parts are the missing positive target, the second engine and the softened copies. Morphs enter through one image-level rule: map energy above that of the warp-only image of the same host by a margin. The graded-mixing set adds that energy must not fall as the mixing fraction rises.
ideas.why_shortcut_free: Cannot use warp (the warp-only image of the same host is a zero target) or softness (softened copies are zero targets): read on the R0-to-R2w shift per engine and the native-to-softened shift. Unseen engines play the role of unseen attack types. The softness floor is not removed by construction and must be reported as before.
ideas.used_in_morph_detection_already: Two-sided pixel-wise supervision exists (PW-MAD, Damer et al., ISVC 2021, arXiv 2108.10291, taken from George and Marcel's anti-spoofing work). One-class morph detectors exist (SPL-MAD arXiv 2208.05787, MAD-DDPM arXiv 2306.15733, SRL-MAD arXiv 2603.15050). A map regressed to zero on genuine images with free morphs was not found. Searches: "face morphing attack detection one-class anomaly detection bona fide only"; "PW-MAD pixel-wise supervision generalized face morphing attack detection".
ideas.first_test: One day, CPU after tokens, alpha-field training set and landmark ladder. Two heads on identical tokens: the current ridge fit to the measured target and the one-sided head (absolute-value loss to zero on genuine constructions, hinge on image energy within host). Read the registered controls: R0-to-R2w shift per engine, softened-genuine shift, and the within-image rank correlation of the predicted map with the true field on gradient and bump images. PASS: R0-to-R2w shift at most 0.3 standard deviations on both engines and correlation at least 0.2. KILL: the shift on FaceMorpher stays above 0.3 (now 0.73), or the correlation is below 0.2; then it is a global flag and not a map.
ideas.risk: With only an image-level rule for morphs the head has little reason to localise. A two-person morph has 0.52 times the detail energy of its halves and the softened copies may not match that level, so the softness route can stay open. It improves a component that is no longer the headline of the paper.

does_not_transfer: Temporal, physiological and interactive cues (pulse, motion, challenge-response): we have one still image, and a morph is not a recapture, both classes were photographed live.
Depth, reflection and moire targets: they describe a flat or screen surface, which a morph does not have; the matching dense target for us is local blend evidence, already on the table.

Context cues (frame, hands, bezel): real attack evidence in anti-spoofing, but in an enrolment portrait anything outside the inner face is a data-set cue; only the with-and-without control design transfers.

Leave-one-data-set-out as practised: it assumes each data set holds both classes from one capture pipeline. In morph benchmarks the shortcut separates the classes inside each data set (a file attribute in all 17 cells), so holding a data set out does not expose it; environments must be interventions on one photo, which is the ladder.
Symmetric domain invariance of both classes (2019 style): the field itself left it, and landmark, GAN and diffusion morphs differ more than print and replay.

Test-time adaptation with model updates (Huang et al., BMVC 2023): needs a stream of unlabelled target data, moves the threshold during use and breaks the one-fixed-network rule; only update-free style projection transfers.
Fusion of algorithms and video input: both help in the NIST test, both are forbidden by our constraints.

Quality-conditioned decisions (quality score fed to the network as in DiffFAS, or a threshold that depends on file size): a gate in spirit, and the one morph-detection trial of a file-size-dependent threshold 'does not help much' (Marriott, NIST IFPC 2025).
Image-level frequency-band masking and high-frequency branches: they need new filtering code, and frequency residuals are the most history-sensitive features we know.

Cue-simulating augmentation (moire overlays, colour changes) and class-specific resampling as used by challenge winners: outside the allowed image operations, and resampling one class is how a resolution shortcut is planted.

Identity suppression as a goal (patch swapping between subjects, orthogonal identity features): in anti-spoofing the face is incidental, in morph detection the second identity defines the attack; identity-free training transfers only as a reference, a role our paired-differences experiment already plays.

Language supervision by class name: zero-shot CLIP is near chance for anti-spoofing (FoundPAD Table 1) and FLIP's own ablation puts most of the gain in the image-encoder weights, which the MADation recipe already uses.
Scoring habits of the academic table: HTER at the test set's own EER threshold and best-snapshot reporting hide the failure we measure and must not be imported.

analyses.field: Deepfake detection (face swap, reenactment, face editing): detection of manipulated face images and video frames
lessons: Detectors trained on blends of real images are blend detectors, not identity detectors. Self-blended images (one image blended with a moved copy of itself, labelled fake) reach 93.18 AUC on Celeb-DF without seeing a deepfake (Shiohara and Yamasaki, CVPR 2022, Table 1). This matches our paired-difference result that a head trained only on one-person mixes ranks two-person morphs at 0.78.

The label of a composite of real material decides everything. In ED4 (Cheng et al., arXiv 2408.06779) composites of real faces labelled real give 0.8195 average cross-dataset AUC; left out 0.6832 (Table VII); labelled fake 0.6061 / 0.5419 / 0.5351 on three sets (Table IV), because the detector 'mistakenly takes the ClockMix splicing patterns as the indicator of forgery'. This is direct outside evidence for one-person blends as negatives.

Pooling different kinds of fake into one class hurts; ordering them helps. ProDet (Cheng et al., NeurIPS 2024): adding real deepfakes to blend-only training lowers average cross-dataset AUC from 0.807 to 0.781 (Table 2); cumulative attribute bits (blending clue, identity inconsistency, generative artefact) with bridging between neighbouring anchors give 0.8225 against 0.7814 for self-blending (Table 1).

A face swap puts two sources in two places; a morph puts them in the same place. Blending boundary (Face X-ray, Li et al., CVPR 2020, target 4M(1-M)), patch self-consistency (Zhao et al., ICCV 2021) and inner-against-outer identity (Dong et al., CVPR 2022) all need a second region. A full-face morph has none, so these targets are constant unless we build the second region in training.

Pair every fake with its own real and treat both the same. Self-blending applies the same augmentation to a real image and its blend; GenD (Yermakov et al., WACV 2026, Table S1) gets 90.0 against 85.3 mean AUROC over 14 benchmarks from paired against unpaired training splits of the same size.

Binary detectors silently learn identity. A linear probe on frozen detector features recognises persons, and the identity-driven part of the score helps in-dataset (AUC 81.5 to 99.6 on FaceForensics++) and hurts across datasets (44.4 to 49.5 on Celeb-DF) (Dong et al., CVPR 2023, Table 1). With five partner faces in all SMDD morphs this is a live risk for us.

High AUC hides threshold failure. GenD's supplement shows mean AUROC 91.2 with true-positive rate at 1% false positives from 10.9% to 92.3% across datasets (Tables S4 to S7); the Deepfake Detection Challenge winner fell from 82.56% on the public set to 65.18% on the hidden set (Meta AI report, 2020).

The generalisation tables of 2025 and 2026 are led by a CLIP-class encoder with a very small adaptation: Effort (Yan et al., arXiv 2411.15633, Table 1) 0.917 average; GenD 91.2 to 91.6 over 14 sets against 88.5 and 88.4 for Effort and Forensics Adapter under equal data (Table 4). Full fine-tuning collapses the feature space (effective rank 160 to 57, Effort Table 8). MADation is already in this family; architecture is not our lever.

Identity-reading detectors are robust to degradation but need an explicit consistency loss and are bound to their training population. The Identity Consistency Transformer stays high under JPEG down to quality 20 (Dong et al., CVPR 2022, Figure 5) and drops to 51.48 on Celeb-DF v2 without its consistency loss; an independent benchmark found it much weaker on non-celebrities (Le et al., EuroS&P 2025, institutional summary).

Everything blend-based is silent on fully synthesised faces: self-blending 69.11 AUC on StyleGAN faces (its Section 5), 0.342 and 0.426 on entire-face synthesis in DF40 (Yan et al., NeurIPS 2024, Table 5); Face X-ray, Zhao et al. and the test-time method OST state the same limit. Our GAN and diffusion-autoencoder morphs are that case.
shortcut_findings: Resolution with the wrong sign: in DF40 the real training data are sharper than the fakes, detectors learn 'low resolution implies fake', and AUC on a sharp unseen fake set is 0.006 for Xception (Yan et al., NeurIPS 2024, Table 5). Remedy there: a benchmark with the same real data for 40 forgery methods and separate protocols for new forgery and new data domain.

Compression removes blend evidence: Face X-ray falls from 87.35 to 61.6 AUC from light to heavy compression (Li et al., CVPR 2020, Section 6). Remedy: QAD trains one model on several quality versions of the same image and ties their representations (Le and Woo, ICCV 2023).

Identity leakage: binary detectors encode identity without supervision, which helps in-dataset and hurts across datasets (Dong et al., CVPR 2023, Figure 2 and Table 1). Remedy: an anchor-based module that decides on local windows, trained with multi-scale window swaps between a fake and its source.

Content, position and seam bias: ED4 (Cheng et al., arXiv 2408.06779) splices sectors of several faces and labels composites of real faces real; without them 0.8195 falls to 0.6832 (Table VII), labelled fake it falls to 0.54 to 0.61 (Table IV). Token shuffling and mixing addresses position and content bias (Fu et al., arXiv 2501.04376). Liang et al. (ECCV 2022) built unbalanced datasets to measure content bias.

Background and pairing: paired training (each fake shares the background video of a real) beats unpaired training on all 14 benchmarks, mean 90.0 against 85.3 (Yermakov et al., WACV 2026, Table S1); the shortcut reading is the authors' interpretation.

Method fingerprints as a low-rank subspace: keeping only the 'method-sensitive subspace' of the features retains most in-domain AUC and collapses on unseen domains (Wang et al., arXiv 2606.01843, Figure 2b). Remedy: gradient projection away from it in training and neuron scaling at inference (0.3774 to 0.9066 in one cell, Table 1); the two remedies are not additive.

Irregular swaps: swaps across gender or race tie the look of a face to 'fake'; detectors trained on Face X-ray's blended images developed systematic group bias, gaps up to 10.7% (Trinh and Liu, IJCAI 2021).

Hidden and in-the-wild test sets reorder results: Deepfake Detection Challenge 82.56% public against 65.18% hidden (Meta AI, 2020); open detectors lose about 45 to 50% of AUC on media circulated in 2024 (Chandra et al., arXiv 2503.02857). Preprocessing differences make comparisons unfair (DeepfakeBench, arXiv 2307.01426) and reproduced numbers differ from published ones (GenD Table 5).

Leakage sinks claims: 'The Alpha Blending Hypothesis' (Yermakov et al., arXiv 2605.10334), which called frame-level detectors 'alpha blending searchers', was withdrawn on 4 Nov 2026 because training photos overlapped test sets.

A blind baseline found a spurious cue: leading silence alone separates real from fake in two audio-visual datasets; the remedy was training on real data only (Smeu et al., CVPR 2025, arXiv 2412.00175).

ideas.name: Second-identity field with a one-person blend as its complement
ideas.source_technique: Dense localisation targets of Face X-ray (Li et al., CVPR 2020) and pairwise self-consistency learning (Zhao et al., ICCV 2021); per-region identity labels of the Identity Consistency Transformer (Dong et al., CVPR 2022); 'composites of real material are real' from ED4 (Cheng et al., arXiv 2408.06779).
ideas.transfer: A face swap has a free reference region (the outer face); a morph has none, so we build one and make it equally blended. For host H, a second photo H' of the same person and a partner P: run the existing alpha-field wrapper on (H', P) with a spatial field (sector, half, gradient), giving a second layer Q that is the same person in one part and the other person elsewhere; then run the same wrapper on (H, Q) at a uniform 0.5, which equals the unchanged tool. Every pixel is then a 50% blend of the host with a warped second layer; the parts differ only in whose face the second layer is. The target map is the field; uniform images keep labels (R0, R1, R2w, R3m, R3 zero, R4 one). The existing shrink-and-enlarge path is applied after compositing to a random half. For a share of composites the second-layer weight is 0.5 on the one-person part and 0.25 to 0.3 on the two-person part, so fine-detail softness is crossed with the target. One network: a dense head on patch tokens beside the classifier, per-patch loss plus pairwise-consistency loss, image score is the pooled field.
ideas.why_shortcut_free: Inside one training image storage history, border, capture detail and host expression are identical in both parts; both parts are 50% blends and both second layers are warped twice; fine-detail softness is crossed by the weight field; seam-only composites (two one-person parts, or two two-person parts) carry a constant target. Ladder contrasts that show it: the pooled field must not move from R0 to R1 or from R0 to R2w (limit 0.3 standard deviations, at most 10% of history-matched genuine photos flagged), and must separate R3 from R4.
ideas.used_in_morph_detection_already: Not in this form. Pixel-wise supervision with a constant map exists (PW-MAD, Damer et al., ISVC 2021, arXiv 2108.10291); partial morphs whose untouched part is the original photo exist (Seibold et al., JISA 2020, arXiv 1806.04265); our own alpha-field probe contrasts blended with unblended. No partial morph with a same-person-blend complement, and no dataset with morph masks, found in searches 'morphing attack detection Face X-ray OR blending boundary OR pixel-wise supervision' and 'morph localization pixel-level morphed regions partial morph dataset 2024 2025 2026'.
ideas.first_test: One day: build 2,000 composites from the landmark ladder hosts with the alpha-field wrapper (CPU, about 1,165 images per minute), extract DINOv3 patch tokens at 512, fit the ridge patch head of the alpha-field probe on the new target, 5 folds by person. Pass: within-image AUC (two-person part against one-person part) at least 0.75; pooled R3 against R4 at least 0.85 with lower bound above 0.80; shifts R0 to R2w and R0 to R1 at most 0.3 standard deviations. Kill: within-image AUC below 0.60, or below 0.55 on the softness-crossed composites, or a warp-only shift above 0.5 standard deviations on the OpenCV-style engine.
ideas.risk: Real morphs are uniform, so at test time the head must work from absolute evidence. The second layer is interpolated twice and the whole composite carries a quarter of the partner's shape. Running the wrapper twice is a new use of approved code and needs the author's yes; the class of a composite is a ruling. Silent by design on generator morphs.

ideas.name: Cumulative ladder code instead of one morph label
ideas.source_technique: ProDet: ordered anchors real, self-blend, cross-identity blend, deepfake with cumulative attribute bits, attribute-steered attention and feature bridging between neighbouring anchors (Cheng et al., 'Can We Leave Deepfake Data Behind in Training Deepfake Detector?', NeurIPS 2024, arXiv 2408.17052).
ideas.transfer: Our rungs are that ordered path. One network gets three cumulative bits (geometry moved; two captures superposed; second person) plus a nuisance bit for storage history, with every rung also present with history. R0 and R1 are 000, R2w is 100, R3m and R3 are 110, R4 is 111; graded-mixing images give the third bit a soft label that rises with the mixing fraction. For generator ladders the first two bits read 'is a render' and 'two codes mixed' and the third bit is shared. The attack score is the third bit alone; the second bit is reported as single-subject manipulation, which is the class proposal awaiting the author. From ProDet we take joint training with attention steered by the bits, and bridging only between neighbours (real graded mixes, and feature mixes of R3 and R4 of one host). ProDet argues that a one-hot multi-class label cannot give this order.
ideas.why_shortcut_free: One-person blends are explicit negatives of the attack bit, so warp, blending and 'softer than a photo' all occur at label 0; storage history has its own bit and is crossed with the others. Ladder contrasts: the attack bit must separate R4 from R3 and from R3m and must not move from R0 to R1 or to R2w.
ideas.used_in_morph_detection_already: None found. Search 'morphing attack detection ordinal OR progressive OR multi-label attributes same-identity morph OR self-morph negative class' returned only SelfMAD (self-blends labelled attack, arXiv 2504.05504) and Kashiani et al. (same-person morphs as attack augmentation, arXiv 2308.10392). Pimenta et al. (BIOSIG 2023, arXiv 2309.00549) label same-person morphs genuine, a binary choice.
ideas.first_test: Hours on cached mean patch tokens (DINOv3 at 512, CLIP at 224) of the landmark ladder: three logistic bits, 5 folds by person, one engine held out; the new probe is two-person morphs against all one-person rungs. Reference: the two-person head of the paired-difference experiment gives R3 against R4 0.759. Pass: third bit R3 against R4 and R3m against R4 at least 0.85 (lower bounds above 0.80), R2w against R4 at least 0.95, shifts R0 to R1 and R0 to R2w at most 0.3 standard deviations, excess over the best simple statistic at least 0.05. Kill: R3 against R4 below 0.80, or excess below 0.05, or more than 20% of history-matched genuine photos flagged.
ideas.risk: On frozen features the code is three separate probes, so any gain from joint training shows only in a LoRA fit (second step: halve the storage-history rise at no more than 2 points of native EER). ProDet uses frame-aligned versions of one image; our rungs have different shapes. The third bit is weak for look-alike pairs and, by theory, for generator morphs (0.65 measured).

ideas.name: History-subspace surgery: audit released detectors by projection, then keep gradients out of the subspace
ideas.source_technique: Shortcut-subspace suppression S3: probe, singular directions, projection test, null-space gradient projection and neuron scaling (Wang et al., 'Suppressing Forgery-Specific Shortcuts for Generalizable Deepfake Detection', arXiv 2606.01843); QAD's tying of quality versions (Le and Woo, ICCV 2023); latent-space augmentation (Yan et al., CVPR 2024).
ideas.transfer: The subspace comes from interventions, not labels: leading directions of the feature differences R1 minus R0 and R2w minus R0 at the layer before the head. Step A is an audit: for each released detector whose features we can read, keep the head and score twice, with only the part of the features inside the subspace (S3's Figure 2b test) and with that part removed. If the benchmark is still solved from the subspace alone, or if removing it lowers false alarms but raises benchmark error strongly, the published number rested on directions that storage history moves; this is causal evidence at feature level beside our image-level interventions. Step B is a training rule: in the LoRA fit project the gradient at that layer away from the subspace, re-estimated each epoch from fixed photo pairs. A second arm adds sampled history differences to the features of both classes. No pixel operation is created; only existing processed files are used.
ideas.why_shortcut_free: By construction for the measured directions (storage history, warp). The check is the ladder on a photo pool not used to estimate the subspace: the score must not move from R0 to R1 or to R2w, and R3 against R4 must be kept.
ideas.used_in_morph_detection_already: None found. Search 'morphing attack detection null space OR gradient projection OR subspace projection OR concept erasure' returned nothing in morph detection (closest: consistency regularisation, Kashiani et al., arXiv 2308.10392). It extends our own round-1 idea of a paired head with interventional nulling; new are the audit use on released detectors and the gradient rule for LoRA training.
ideas.first_test: One day of scoring and linear algebra: estimate the subspace on one photo pool at rank 1, 2, 4, 8, 16; apply to the retrained MADation recipe and our heads; evaluate on a second photo pool, the FRLL landmark cells and the landmark ladder. Pass: at some rank of at most 16 the flag rate of history-matched genuine photos falls by at least half while native EER on landmark cells rises by at most 2 points. Kill (training rule): no rank up to 16 lowers the flag rate by at least a quarter. An EER rise above 5 points with falling flags is the audit's finding, not a kill.
ideas.risk: Linear and at one layer; a LoRA fit can move the cue elsewhere. S3 itself is a single-dataset preprint with single runs and reports that its two remedies are not additive (over-attenuation). The frozen-encoder failure in our record warns that the cue may be spread over many directions.

ideas.name: Identity-agreement slots with a partner-retrieval test
ideas.source_technique: Identity Consistency Transformer: two identity vectors from one image, consistency loss, distance as the score (Dong et al., 'Protecting Celebrities from DeepFake with Identity Consistency Transformer', CVPR 2022, arXiv 2203.01318); explicit against implicit identity (Huang et al., CVPR 2023); DiffusionFake, where a real image's two reconstruction targets are the image itself (Sun et al., NeurIPS 2024).
ideas.transfer: This upgrades the two-contributor embedding head already in our plan rather than replacing it. First, consistent means 'one person', not 'unprocessed': for R0, R1, R2w, R3m and R3 both slots are pulled to the host's face-recognition embedding; for R4 the slots go to the two contributors' embeddings in either order. Second, the score is the distance between the two slots: one network, one image, one number. Third, a falsifier that needs no detector: on held-out two-person morphs the second slot must retrieve the true partner among held-out persons. If the slots separate R3 from R4 but cannot find the partner, they are not reading identity. The Identity Consistency Transformer shows why the consistency class matters: without its consistency loss it falls to 51.48 AUC on Celeb-DF v2.
ideas.why_shortcut_free: Targets are face-recognition embeddings of the source photos, which storage history, warp and blending do not change; one-person blends sit inside the consistent class. Ladder contrasts: slot distance must rise from R3 to R4 and must not rise from R0 to R1, R2w or R3m; the retrieval test shows what the distance is made of.
ideas.used_in_morph_detection_already: Partly. Two identity vectors exist in OrthoMAD (Neto et al., arXiv 2208.07841) and its successor (Caldeira et al., EUSIPCO 2023, arXiv 2306.03002), trained on SMDD without a one-person-blend class and without a retrieval test. Inner-against-outer identity and demorphing used as a detector were not found (searches 'morphing attack detection identity consistency OR inner face outer face single image' and 'single-image face demorphing used as morph detector reference-free').
ideas.first_test: Hours on cached patch tokens of the landmark ladder with the existing ArcFace embeddings of the sources: a two-slot head, 5 folds by person, one engine held out. Pass: R3 against R4 at least 0.80, true partner in the top 5 for at least 20% of held-out morphs among at least 100 held-out persons (chance 5%), shifts R0 to R1 and R0 to R2w at most 0.3 standard deviations. Kill: partner in the top 5 for at most 10%, or R3 against R4 below 0.70.
ideas.risk: Needs many partners: on SMDD as released the second slot can memorise five faces (identity leakage in our setting). For generator morphs the slots can at best read how average the face is. An identity reader can be bound to its training population. Lower priority if the first two ideas pass.

does_not_transfer: Blending-boundary target (Face X-ray): the map 4M(1-M) is constant inside a full-face morph; it exists only for spliced morphs, and a detector for one construction is a gate by another name.

Self-blends labelled as attacks (self-blended images, SelfMAD): the label breaks our rule that a processed genuine image is not a morph, and the signal is 'two layers' plus softness, which storage history imitates.

Patch self-consistency and source features (Zhao et al.; sensor-noise methods): every patch of a uniform blend has the same mix, so there is nothing to contrast; sensor traces are unlikely to survive the shrink-and-enlarge history (not tested).

Inner-against-outer identity (Identity Consistency Transformer, Nirkin et al.): needs an untouched surround from one contributor; only spliced morphs have it and tight crops remove it. Usable at most as an audit probe for spliced-morph cells.

Frequency methods (F3-Net, high-frequency noise features, phase-spectrum learning, FreqBlender): they read generator up-sampling (for us the generator fingerprint, shared by a one-person reconstruction) or the spectral change of a blend (our softness floor). Phase-only or spectrum-flattened inputs do not help, because storage at 63 to 65 pixels removes the bands and flattening amplifies the residue.

Reconstruction and real-only anomaly detection (RECCE, SeeABLE, Real Appearance Modeling, muFlow): 'not like a camera photo' fires on R1, R2w and one-photo reconstructions, which are genuine for us; once those are in the normal class a two-person morph is barely anomalous.

Test-time training on a pseudo-fake built from the test image (OST): the references inherit whatever the test image contains; the measurable step shrinks only by a factor 0.87 if the image is already a two-person morph, which is the weak identity-shrinkage statistic again. Its authors also exclude fully synthesised images.
Online test-time adaptation over a stream (T2A; in morph detection Di Domenico et al., FG 2026): not one image.
Reference-based identity checks (Identity Consistency Transformer with a reference set, FACTOR, ID-Reveal): need a claimed identity or reference media, which is the differential setting.
Video, temporal and physiological cues (blood-flow signals, lip-sync, motion): one still image.
Ensembles and side-by-side detectors (challenge winners, TrueMedia, the withdrawn 94.0% ensemble): forbidden by the one-network constraint.

Identity-unaware design with local anchors (Dong et al., CVPR 2023): removes identity, the one thing we want, and leaves local texture where the softness cue lives; only its identity probe transfers, as a diagnostic.

Training only the residual subspace of pretrained weights (Effort): steers learning toward what the pretrained model treats as minor detail, which is where our history cue lives; only the lesson about feature-rank collapse transfers.
Any blend-based method for GAN or diffusion-autoencoder morphs: they are entire-face synthesis from a mixed code, where the blend family is silent in the deepfake field too.

analyses.field: Detection of fully GAN-generated images (faces above all), 2019 to 2026
lessons: Data design now beats architecture. The leading generalisation rows of 2024 to 2026 use an ordinary pretrained encoder trained on pairs where each fake is a reconstruction of a real image: B-Free 96.3% average balanced accuracy over 27 generators, 20.7 points above the second best (Guillaro et al., CVPR 2025, arXiv 2412.17671, Table 5); Dual Data Alignment 90.7% over 11 benchmarks, 15.7 points above the second best (Chen et al., NeurIPS 2025, arXiv 2505.14359, Table 2). The same RINE architecture goes from 65.0 to 83.2% when only the training data change (B-Free, Table 4).

The published GAN morph cells measure generated-image detection. A ResNet-50 trained only on ProGAN images, never on a morph, reaches EER 0.00 / 0.56 / 0.00% on FRLL-StyleGAN2, FRGC-StyleGAN2 and FRGC-MIPGAN, and its authors call GAN-morph detection 'strongly equivalent' to GAN-image detection (Colbois and Marcel, BIOSIG 2022, arXiv 2209.00404, Table 2). Venkatesh et al. (IWBF 2020, arXiv 2007.03621, Table II) already detected StyleGAN morphs at 0 to 0.68% EER with simple detectors.

A midpoint of two latent codes is, to second order, a truncated single code. The midpoint has half the variance per coordinate, and for a Gaussian prior multiplying by sqrt(2) gives back the prior exactly (Agustsson et al., ICLR 2019, arXiv 1711.01970). Truncation w' = w_mean + psi (w - w_mean) is visible in images: quality up, variation down (Karras et al. 2019, arXiv 1812.04948), precision up and recall down (Kynkaanniemi et al. 2019, arXiv 1904.06991, Figure 5). So our 0.89 to 0.94 is a truncation reading, and near-chance against spread-matched renders is the predicted outcome of a correct control.

Midpoints look real, so no realism or reproducibility test flags them: of 500,000 straight paths in W with both ends on the real manifold only 2.4% cross unrealistic regions (Kynkaanniemi et al. 2019). Projection tests answer 'did this generator make it' (Karras et al. 2020, arXiv 1912.04958, Section 5), which is yes for a morph and for a one-person render alike.

W is not Gaussian, so the 'nothing beyond radius' argument is exact only in a Gaussianised space. Every mapping layer ends in a leaky ReLU; W marginals are 'heavily skewed'; even after undoing the last leaky ReLU and whitening only 219 of 512 marginals pass a normality test; a normal fitted to W gives FID 76.63 against 3.28 in the Gaussianised space (Zhu et al. 2020, arXiv 2012.09036; Wulff and Torralba 2020, arXiv 2009.06529). Inverted codes also lie off the sampled distribution (Tov et al. 2021, arXiv 2102.02766). Higher-order traces of linear mixing are therefore possible in principle and untested.

Frozen foundation features are not protection. A frozen-CLIP detector moves with resize direction (accuracy on real images 54.16 to 83.58% when they are downsampled; Rajan et al., ICLR 2025, arXiv 2410.11835, Table 5), and on aligned data a linear probe reaches 68.5% balanced accuracy against 95.2% for end-to-end training (B-Free, Table 3).

A feature extractor pretrained to recognise image processing separates a morph benchmark. DNA-Det is pretrained to classify 170 kinds of compression, blur, resampling and noise (Yang et al., AAAI 2022, arXiv 2202.13843); its features give 0.87 / 0.82 / 0.48% one-class EER on landmark, GAN and diffusion morphs of FRGC (Colbois and Marcel, IJCB 2024, arXiv 2410.16802, Table 7).

A fixed threshold is the hard part and published numbers do not predict behaviour on new data. 'Accuracy results are much less encouraging, since a fixed threshold is used' and 2x downsampling is 'catastrophic' (Gragnaniello et al. 2021, arXiv 2104.02617). In a 2026 zero-shot study of 23 released detectors the best reaches 75.0% mean accuracy and training-data alignment causes 20 to 60% variance within identical architectures (Ren et al., arXiv 2602.07814, abstract).

Attackers already use norm-preserving interpolation. MLSD-GAN builds morphs by spherical interpolation of StyleGAN latents (Reddy et al., arXiv 2404.12679, abstract), so averageness is a detector of naive latent morphs only.

Each bias fix exposed the next one: format, then size, then resize direction, then a frequency band (Grommelt et al. 2024; Rajan et al. 2025; Chen et al. 2025). None of these papers claims a cue-free training set. A ladder of matched controls should be the training set as well as the instrument.
shortcut_findings: Format as label. In GenImage real images are JPEG (mostly quality 96) and fakes are PNG. A Midjourney-trained ResNet-50 calls uncompressed real FFHQ photos real in 80.45% of cases; after JPEG at quality 95 / 90 / 80 / 60 this is 94.84 / 98.93 / 99.95 / 100% (Grommelt et al., 'Fake or JPEG?', arXiv 2403.17608, Table 2).
